body.statement:
At the selected-law factorization level, \(\mathfrak M\) is the finite four-response-type specialization of Condition 1 of Shingaki--Yoshida--Kuroki (2026).  Design A, \(\mathcal F_A(p,m)\), is the subfiber obtained by fixing the population cell margin \(m\); consequently Theorem 1 of that paper transfers to the regular design-A domain by restriction.  Design B, \(\mathcal F_B(p)\), is the equation-(13) IV subclass with the additional relevance inequality; consequently Corollary 1 transfers directly to its regular domain.  On every such regular observable law for which the applicable full fiber is nonempty, the fiber is rigid and \(\mathscr A\) returns the corresponding published PN/PS value, including the Appendix formulas (A.28)--(A.33) where they apply.

The atlas additionally classifies every compatible observable law in the singular or boundary complement of those regular domains, including design-A rank loss, coincident endpoints, inactive rows, and forced-zero incident coefficients, and the analogous design-B residual-forest strata.  It returns either an exact target-rigidity certificate or a legal target-changing full-SCM pair.  An empty fiber is reported separately as incompatibility.  This is a strict extension of the compatible classification domain to singular and boundary strata; it is not an extension of the published regular formula beyond its hypotheses and is not a blanket subsumption claim.
body.justification: The theorem distinguishes design-A transfer by restriction of Theorem 1 from direct design-B transfer of equation (13) and Corollary 1.
body.gap: The published regular results do not classify the compatible singular and boundary complement or incompatible inputs.
body.consumer: Users can separate exact regular agreement, singular/boundary rigidity, nonidentification, and incompatibility without a formula-extension or subsumption claim.
body.proof_tex:
The factorization comparison in \(\mathrm{lem:shingaki\text{-}yoshida\text{-}kuroki\text{-}design\text{-}transfer}\) identifies the exact relationship between the two model descriptions.  Under \(P_{\vartheta}\in\mathfrak M\), response consistency restricts a selected cell \(e\) to the two types in \(\mathcal I_e\), proxy exclusion supplies one shared proxy kernel \(b_i\) for each type, and outcome-dependent selection contributes only a cell-specific factor.  Thus the selected law is the four-state response-type specialization of their Condition-1 factorization.  Requiring \(P_{\vartheta}(E)=m\) changes neither that factorization nor its regular identifying equations, so \(\mathcal F_A(p,m)\) is a fixed-margin subfiber.  Requiring \(Z\perp U\) imposes their equation-(13) common-\(Z\) restriction, while \(Z\not\!\perp X\) is exactly the additional relevance inequality in the present design-B fiber.

Let \(R_A(p)\) be the PN/PS pair supplied by Theorem 1 and Appendix equations (A.28)--(A.33) on the regular design-A domain.  By the cited transfer lemma, every \(\vartheta\in\mathcal F_A(p,m)\) satisfies
\[
 \tau(\vartheta)=R_A(p).                                   \tag{27}
\]
This is restriction: fixing \(m\) merely selects a subset of the Condition-1 fiber.  If the subfiber is nonempty, (27) holds for all its members, and hence \(\mathcal T_A(p,m)=\{R_A(p)\}\).

Similarly, let \(R_B(p)\) denote the Corollary-1 value on the regular equation-(13) domain.  The cited lemma applies directly to every member of \(\mathcal F_B(p)\), so
\[
 \tau(\vartheta)=R_B(p)
 \quad\hbox{for every }\vartheta\in\mathcal F_B(p),         \tag{28}
\]
and nonemptiness gives \(\mathcal T_B(p)=\{R_B(p)\}\).  The relevance requirement only restricts this identified equation-(13) fiber and therefore cannot change its common value.

By \(\mathrm{thm:full\text{-}rigidity\text{-}atlas}\), a nonempty fiber with either singleton target set in (27)--(28) passes every chartwise disagreement test and returns its unique value.  This proves agreement separately for regular design A and regular design B.

Outside the regular hypotheses, \(\mathrm{thm:mixed\text{-}support\text{-}elimination\text{-}complete}\) proves that the chart family still exhausts every compatible rank-one or rank-two cycle factorization, including all named support faces and all design-B residual forests.  The full-rigidity theorem then returns the common exact target if every disagreement refinement is empty, and otherwise returns two target-changing full SCMs.  Equations (24)--(25) show that an empty chart union is reported as incompatibility before rigidity is asserted.

The extension of the compatible classification domain is strict.  Indeed, let \(\ell=|\mathcal W|\), \(k=|\mathcal Z|\), and choose
\[
 \pi_i=\frac14,\qquad b_i(w)=\frac1\ell,\qquad
 g_i(z)=\frac1k,\qquad e_i(z)=\frac12,\qquad s_e=\frac12
\]
for every admissible index.  These normalized nonnegative mechanisms lie in \(\Theta\), obey response consistency, proxy exclusion, and outcome-dependent selection, and have \(c=1/2>0\).  Each observed cell has two incident response types, so direct multiplication gives
\[
 m_e=\frac14,\qquad
 p_{ewz}=\frac1{4k\ell}>0,
 \qquad T_e(w,z)=\frac1{k\ell}.
\]
Thus the resulting design-A fiber is compatible, while every \(T_e\) has rank one.  The regular proxy matrices therefore fail the invertibility requirement recorded in the cited design-transfer lemma, so this law lies outside the published regular domain but inside the atlas domain.  Finally, no step evaluates \(R_A\) or \(R_B\) after a regular denominator, rank, or separation condition fails; hence the additional conclusion strictly extends the compatible classification domain only, not the published formulas.
